title: Porter & Machery 2024, Scientific Reports 14:26133 (via PsyPost summary; PMC full text blocked by reCAPTCHA)
rule: Non-expert US panelists (n=1634 detection, n=696 rating) judged AI poems human at below-chance accuracy (46.6%, per search summary) and rated them higher on rhythm and beauty. AI poems were ChatGPT-3.5 imitations of 10 named poets, human poems chosen from a database avoiding each poet's most famous. All participants lay; no expert group. Authors' explanation: AI simplicity is easier for non-experts; complex human verse is misread as incoherence. So lay 'can you tell' and 'is it good' judgments do not validate verse; use poetry readers.
llm_tell: Simple, readily legible, rhythmic verse is what lay readers rate well, so it is not evidence of quality for a poetry audience.

title: Portsmouth Grammar School: Can You Tell A Human Poet From AI?
rule: A critic reading ChatGPT imitations of Byron, Whitman, Plath and Ginsberg found: weak rhymes ('beneath'/'relief'), rhyme scheme drifting mid-poem (AABB to ABAB), a stray line breaking the meter, very few figurative techniques (themes stated outright), overcooked platitudes, mixed metaphor. Single critic, not measured.
example: "I'm a fragile, broken yolk" (fake Plath, called confusing); "there are very few figurative techniques actually used"
llm_tell: States the theme outright instead of imaging it; rhyme chosen for sound-alike not sense; scheme and meter slip partway.

title: Walsh, Preus, Gronski: Does ChatGPT Have a Poetic Style? (CHR 2024)
rule: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 poems (5.7k, 24 forms, ~40 subjects) vs 3.7k human poems from Poetry Foundation/Academy of American Poets: 'much more constrained and uniform than human poetry'. Favoured rhyme, four-line stanzas, iambic meter, first-person plural, and the words heart, embrace, echo, whisper. Read via abstract page summary (PDF unreadable by fetcher), so quotes are secondhand.
llm_tell: Rhymed quatrains in iambic rhythm by default; 'we/us/our'; heart/embrace/echo/whisper vocabulary.

title: Search-result summary of rhyme and meter rates in GPT poems (study not identified)
rule: Per a search summary of an unidentified paper: 90.2% of GPT-3.5 poems had at least one rhyme vs 65.0% of Poetry Foundation / Academy of American Poets poems; rhymed lines 63.87% vs 29.45%; dominant iambic meter in about 74% of GPT-3.5 poems vs about 53% of GPT-4 poems. Numbers not verified against the paper; treat as indicative only. Humans rhyme much less, so an LLM's rhyme-by-default is itself a tell.
llm_tell: Rhymes far more often than contemporary published poets; rhyme persists even when asked for free verse (single humanities essay's claim, not controlled).

title: Berklee Online: Pat Pattison on prosody and rhyme
topic: song lyric craft: prosody and rhyme
rule: Prosody is the one rule: 'an appropriate relationship between the elements'. Decide whether the idea is stable or unstable, then make line length, rhythm, melody and rhyme agree with it. Perfect or family rhyme for stable/resolved meaning; assonance and other remote rhymes for unstable/unresolved meaning. Rhyme type is therefore a meaning choice, not decoration. Berklee blog write-up of Pattison; not the book text.
example: Perfect rhyme: identical vowel and following consonants, different starting sound. Family rhyme: same vowel, phonetically related consonants. Assonance: vowels only.
llm_tell: Models use perfect end rhyme uniformly regardless of what the line means, so form never works against or with the idea.

title: Pattison, Writing Better Lyrics: Object Writing (Writer's Digest excerpt)
rule: Object writing: pick a real object at random, write 10 minutes to a timer, using all seven senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, organic, kinesthetic), favouring the unused ones (smell, taste, touch). No rhyme, no rhythm, no complete sentences required; show through sensory detail; leaps to other images allowed. Source material comes from sensory attention to a real thing, before form. The book also has a chapter on clichés (table of contents only; text not read).
llm_tell: Models start from the abstract feeling and the rhyme, not from a perceived object; imagery is stock rather than sensed (heart, whisper, echo).

title: Search-result summaries: poets and critics on ChatGPT poems (Atlantic piece, Ann Arbor Observer, Substacks)
rule: Search summary only, no page read: critics describe ChatGPT verse as riddled with cliche and wince-worthy rhyme, 'too trite and sweet', superficial platitudes, and lacking a lived occasion ('felt necessity'). Opinion, secondhand; no controlled expert-vs-lay comparison was found in this lane. Searches found no study of expert poets' detection rates: a null for 'experts do better', untested.
llm_tell: Sentimental, tidy, platitudinous; no occasion or particular stake behind the poem.
